cit
(‘consciousness’)
------------------------------------------
According to the philosophy of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137), known as Viśiṣṭādvaita (qualified monism), ब्रह्मन्, ईश्वर or God possesses in himself two modes or aspects—the ‘cit’ or the sentient part and the ‘acit’ or the insentient part—using which he brings about च्रेअतिओन्. The innumerable jīvas or individual souls endowed with चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् constitute the ‘cit’ whereas ‘prakṛti’ or insentient nature constitutes ‘acit’.
The word ‘cit’ is also used in other systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् to indicate the सोउल् and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
See also ACIT and VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.

citta
(‘that through which one knows’)
------------------------------------------
‘Citta’ is one of the general names given to the मिन्द् in the Indian philosophical systems. The word ‘manas’ is of course more common. However, since the योग system of पतञ्जलि has adopted this word and treats of it in a technical and exhaustive manner, we will mainly confine ourselves here to the treatment given in that system. As regards the concept of मिन्द् in other systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, see MIND.
Patañjali (200 B.C.) considers ‘citta’ or mindstuff as a physical material made up of the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्, but with a preponderance of सत्त्व. (See GUṆAS, RAJAS, SATTVA and TAMAS.) It is capable of reflecting the power of pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the पुरुष or the individual सोउल्. It is also capable of modifications. It is the modified चित्त with the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् reflected in it that is responsible for चोग्नितिओन्, thinking, doubts or drawing definite conclusions. Hence it is also called by such names as अन्तःकरण (the internal organ), मनस् (the मिन्द्) and बुद्धि (the intellect). The modifications themselves are called ‘cittavṛttis’. When these cittavṛttis are suppressed (‘niruddha’) then, ‘yoga’ results; that is, the पुरुष or the सोउल् gets detached from the चित्त and is re-established in his own glory. ‘Yoga’ (union) is thus actually, ‘viyoga’ (separation) from the mindstuff.
The चित्त works at five levels, called ‘cittabhūmis.’ They are: क्षिप्त (restlessness), mūḍha (torpidity), vikṣipta (distraction), ekāgra (onepointedness) and niruddha (suppressed or without modifications). Of course, it is only in the last two levels that योग is possible.
Patañjali also postulates two ‘citta-dharmas’ or characteristics, for the चित्त. They are paridṛṣṭa (the seen) and aparidṛṣṭa (the unseen). Means of know-ledge like direct perception which rouse cittavṛttis and are hence discernible, belong to the former. ‘Saṁskāras’ or innate tendencies, ‘dharma’ or effects of previous actions inherent in the मिन्द्, ultimately resulting in happy and unhappy experiences and a few other such qualities belong to the second.
Patañjali also deals with some obstacles to योग, called ‘antarāyas’ which cause ‘cittavikṣepa’ or distraction of मिन्द्. व्याधि (disease), स्त्यान (mental laziness), सṁशय (doubt), आलस्य (physical laziness), etc., are some of these obstacles.
To overcome these and get ‘citta-prasādana’ or peace of मिन्द्, he recommends several steps like cultivating an attitude of friendship towards the happy people and compassion towards those in difficulties.
While dealing with the psychic powers, पतञ्जलि mentions ‘cittasaṁvit’ or full knowledge about the मिन्द् by meditating on one’s heart and attaining समाधि (perfect concentration) there.
See also AHAṄKĀRA, ANTAḤKARAṆA, BUDDHI, MANAS and YOGA-DARŚANA.

Citsukha
------------------------------------------
Post-शङ्कर literature on Advaita Vedānta has grown enormously, both in quantity and in quality as also subtlety. चित्सुख is one of the well-known writers of this period, on Advaita Vedānta. He lived in the early part of the thirteenth century. He was a pupil of Gauḍeśvarā-cārya, also known as Jñānottama. His works are: Bhāṣya-भाव-prakāśikā (a commentary on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of शङ्कर); Abhiprāya-prakāśikā (commentary on the ब्रह्मसिद्धि of Maṇḍana); commentaries on the नैष्कर्म्यसिद्धि of सुरेश्वर, Nyāyamakaranda of आनन्द-bodha and खण्डन-खण्ड-खाद्य of श्रीहर्ष.
However his most important work is Tattvapradīpikā, commonly known as Citsukhī. It is a unique work for two reasons:
It effectively refutes the categories of the न्याय-Vaiśeṣika schools;
It establishes some of the fundamental points of शङ्कर’s advaita by carrying out a subtle analysis and interpretation of them.
Citsukhī comprises four chapters. The first chapter deals with the Vedāntic concepts like the आत्मन् being self-luminous and pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, nature of अविद्या (nescience or इग्नोरन्चे), mithyātva (nature of falsity of the world), nature of illusions and so on. The second chapter analyzes the various concepts and categories of the न्याय and the Vaiśeṣika systems like गुण (quality), कर्म (action), सामान्य (generality), समवाय (inherence) and so on, and refutes them. The third chapter deals with the possibility of realization of ब्रह्मन् and the nature of मुक्ति (liberation) through ज्ञान (know-ledge). The last chapter deals with the nature of the ultimate state of लिबेरतिओन्.
See also ADVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.

Citragupta
(‘secret picture’)
------------------------------------------
All the deeds of human beings, whether good or bad, are supposed to be recorded by चित्रगुप्त, the scribe of यम, the god of death. According to one version, he was originally a king of the Sūryavaṁśa (descended from the Sun) who had attained omniscience through the worship of सूर्य. He was hence taken away by यम and appointed as a scribe in his world. As per another version, he emanated out of the body of ब्रह्मा when he was in deep meditation. ब्रह्मा himself taught him the knowledge of the hidden and subtle things. He was later on chosen to be the scribe of यम. He is regarded as the progenitor of the caste ‘kāyastha’ and had nine sons. The names of these sons (eg., भट्ट, नागर, अम्बष्ठ etc.) are also caste names and hence considered as the progenitors of those castes.
Contrary to common conception, चित्रगुप्त is a single person and not two.
Iconographical works depict him as red in colour and place his image to the right of यम. He is invariably shown with a stylus and a palm leaf in his hands, the paraphernalia of a scribe.
Citragupta is worshipped, especially by the kāyasthas (a particular caste), on Yamadvitīyā day (second day of bright half of the month Kārttika, usually in November). On this day sisters invite their brothers for a feast and offer presents.
See also YAMA.

citrāpūrṇimā
(‘full-मोओन् day of चैत्र’)
------------------------------------------
The full-मोओन् day in the month of चैत्र (March-April) is said to be sacred to चित्रगुप्त, the scribe of यम. If the day happens to be a Thursday, Saturday or Sunday, it is considered even more auspicious. Special worship is offered to चित्रगुप्त on this day. In Tamil Nadu, people believe that a bath in the river Citrā rising on the Kuṭṭalam hills in the Tirunelvelly district, on this day, is meritorious since the river took its birth on this day. काञ्चीपुरम् has a temple of चित्रगुप्त, which seems to be the only temple of this deity in the whole of South India.
See also CITRAGUPTA.

Citrāṅgadā
------------------------------------------
Daughter of the king Citravāhana (also known as Malayadhvaja) she was one of the wives of अर्जुन, the great Pāṇḍava hero of the महाभारत. She bore him an equally heroic son, named बभ्रुवाहन. When अर्जुन was on a conquering expedition, following the horse of the अश्वमेध sacrifice, he was challenged and killed by बभ्रुवाहन who did not know him as his ड़थेर्, since बभ्रुवाहन had lived away from him even from childhood days and had no occasion to meet him. चित्राङ्गदा however, revived अर्जुन to life with the help of Ulūpī, another wife of अर्जुन, belonging to the tribe of the नागस्.
See also ARJUNA.

Citrakūṭa
(‘variegated peak’)
------------------------------------------
Citrakūṭa is one of the holy places associated with Śrī राम and an important पिल्ग्रिमगे centre. It is situated in the Banda district of Uttar Pradesh, about 140 kms. (87 miles) from the city of Allahabad.
According to the रामायण of वाल्मीकि, after being banished from अयोध्या, Śrī राम, सीता and लक्ष्मण came here and lived for a few days. It was here that भरत (the brother for whose sake Śrī राम had to give up the kingdom) met him to persuade him to go back to अयोध्या; and failing in the mission, returned with the pādukās (wooden sandals) of Śrī राम.
The poet-saint Tulsīdās (16th cent. A.D.) is said to have had a vision of Śri राम here.
Citrakūṭa and the village Sītāpur are situated on the left bank of the river Mandākinī, also called Payoṣṇī or Payasvinī. It is a very picturesque place with the Kāmadgiri hill and a forest associated with it. It is customary for the pilgrims to go round the hill. This is called ‘parikrama’.
Other notable places are: Rāmghāṭ and Jānakīghaṭ (where Śrī राम and सीता used to bathe); Sphaṭikaśilā (where Śrī राम is said to have slept on the lap of सीता when the demon Kākāsura hurt her); Bharatakūpa (the well into which भरत poured all the sacred waters collected for Śrī राम’s चोरोनतिओन्, but which could not be used); गुप्त-गोदावरी (a stream inside a cave); अत्रि आश्रम, also called Anasūyāji, the hermitage of the sage couple, अत्रि and अनसूया.
Huge crowds gather here on Śrīrāmanavamī (birthday of Śrī राम, usually in April) and दीपावली or Diwali (usually in November) days.
Other holy places in the vicinity of चित्रकूट are the hermitages of वाल्मीकि, शरभङ्ग and सुतीक्ष्ण.

citi
(‘consciousness,’ ‘conscious power’)
------------------------------------------
The योग system of philosophy, as systematized by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) posits three fundamental principles: पुरुष or the individual सोउल्, प्रकृति or insentient nature and ईश्वर or God. Among these, पुरुष is also called by other names such as द्रष्टा (the seer), चिति (consciousness) and citiśakti (conscious power). His essential nature is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्; hence the name.
See also PURUṢA.
